vignette:
Mai, a 48-year-old divorced waitress from a South Eastern Asian background, came to treatment after months of living as if she had been permanently narrowed by a man who would not leave her alone. The stalking had begun after a brief relationship ended, but what made it terrifying was how ordinary moments had become contaminated by his persistence: seeing his car creep past the restaurant after her late shifts, finding missed calls with no message, noticing him waiting near her apartment building when she got home after dark. At first she tried to dismiss it, but the fear settled into her body when she realized he seemed to know her routines. After that, she no longer felt like the woman she had been. She said she used to be happy, but now she was “always miserable,” and more than that, she felt dead inside, as if nothing in her life carried meaning anymore. That conviction that she had been permanently changed kept pulling her back to the stalking in her mind, as if she needed to keep revisiting the moments that had stripped something essential from her life. The more she told herself that her happiness was gone for good, the more the memories seemed to find her on their own.

As the memories kept forcing their way into her mind when she did not want them, Mai became unable to hold the experience at a distance. The scene returned in fragments she could not control: the sound of footsteps behind her, the sight of his face in her hallway light, the sickening realization that she was being watched. She said she could not really put it into words, and when she tried, it felt strangely as if it belonged to someone else rather than to her. Because the memory kept breaking in that way, Mai began building her days around keeping it away. She avoided reminders, shut down conversations about what had happened, and kept herself busy on late shifts so there would be less quiet in which the images could surface. That unsettled quality made the memory harder to settle, not easier; because it felt unreal and alien, she kept turning it over in her head, trying to make it fit, and it intruded even more forcefully. The more it broke in, the more she concluded that something had been stolen from her life that could never be restored.

Those appraisals became the lens through which she organized every day. If she believed her happiness was gone for good and nothing meaningful remained, then even small efforts felt pointless, and she began to avoid seeing people she had socialized with before the stalking began. Former friends from work invited her out, but she declined, sure that she had nothing to offer anymore and that being around them would only remind her of the person she used to be. She also started avoiding looking at or paying attention to her own body. In the mirror she saw an exhausted woman who no longer recognized herself, and the sight only confirmed her belief that she had changed into someone diminished and joyless.

The memory also kept shaping how dangerous the world seemed. Because the event had arrived through ordinary routines and unexpected proximity, Mai now could not trust unfamiliar places; she avoided going anywhere new because she felt unable to assess the danger there. Living with that constant sense of danger slowly hardened into the belief that this was simply how her life was now: unsafe, narrowed, and beyond repair. The threat that shadowed her days became the most convincing proof she had that nothing meaningful or stable would come back. On her walk from the bus stop to the restaurant, she scanned every parked vehicle and doorway, and at home she listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering. A creak in the stairwell or a knock downstairs could send a surge through her chest and stomach, with strong physical reactions that left her shaky and nauseated. Each jolt seemed to confirm that her mind was right to stay on guard. The more she watched for danger, the more real the threat felt, and the more she told herself that life had lost its meaning because safety was no longer something she could assume.

That same fear also narrowed her behavior around other people. Mai avoided any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, even at work, where she often let customers speak sharply without defending herself and asked coworkers to handle difficult tables. As a waitress, she moved through crowded shifts trying not to draw attention, taking the long route to the kitchen and slipping out through familiar doors only. She had come to believe that if she argued, objected, or even appeared difficult, it might provoke someone who would follow her, watch her, or escalate in ways she could not control. Those efforts to stay safe kept the stalking alive in her mind. Every time she checked a doorway or altered her route, the memory came back with more force, as if the very work of keeping it at a distance had only kept it close. In that way, her attempts to stay safe kept bringing the memory back: every cautious detour, every quiet concession, reminded her of why she no longer felt like herself.

By the time she sought help, Mai was exhausted by the tight circle of remembering, fearing, and withdrawing. The stalking had ended, but she still lived as though it might resume at any moment, listening at night for signs of entry and measuring every unfamiliar corner for risk. What brought her in was the realization that her world had shrunk to work, home, and vigilance, and that even those spaces no longer felt secure. She was most afraid that if she stopped monitoring, stopped avoiding, or allowed herself to hope again, she would be caught off guard; at the same time, she was hoping that treatment might help her feel like herself again, before the memory and the fear had taken over everything.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows negative appraisals and intrusive memory, but it does not clearly state that the appraisals drive the memory intrusions.
It describes avoidance and safety behaviors, but not that the memory itself causes or leads to those maladaptive strategies in the same paragraph.
The vignette shows threat and negative appraisals, but it does not clearly say that feeling of threat leads to her negative beliefs or appraisals.
It shows avoidance/safety behaviors and later memory reactivation, but not that the maladaptive strategies themselves bring the memory back or intensify it.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette shows negative appraisals and intrusive memory, but it does not clearly state that the appraisals drive the memory intrusions.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: It describes avoidance and safety behaviors, but not that the memory itself causes or leads to those maladaptive strategies in the same paragraph.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows threat and negative appraisals, but it does not clearly say that feeling of threat leads to her negative beliefs or appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: It shows avoidance/safety behaviors and later memory reactivation, but not that the maladaptive strategies themselves bring the memory back or intensify it.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
